questions.stem: A Banach space is a normed vector space that is:

options.explanation: A Banach space is a complete normed vector space. Completeness is what distinguishes Banach spaces from general normed spaces and makes fixed-point theorems work.
$\mathbb{R}^n$ is a Banach space but functional analysis is primarily about infinite-dimensional Banach spaces like $C([a,b])$ and $L^p$ spaces.
Inner products give Hilbert spaces, which are special cases of Banach spaces. Not every Banach space has an inner product structure.
Compact spaces have special properties not shared by all Banach spaces. The unit ball of an infinite-dimensional Banach space is never compact.

questions.stem: Parseval's theorem in a Hilbert space with orthonormal basis $\{e_n\}$ states:

options.explanation: Parseval's theorem generalises the Pythagorean theorem to infinite dimensions. In Fourier terms: the total energy equals the sum of squared Fourier coefficients.
Missing squares and absolute values. Parseval's theorem involves squared norms and squared absolute values of coefficients.
The reconstruction formula is $f = \sum_n \langle f, e_n\rangle e_n$ — the $e_n$ factor is missing here.
That would require $f$ and $g$ to be parallel (scalar multiples of each other). The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality says $|\langle f,g\rangle| \le \|f\|\|g\|$ with equality iff parallel.

questions.stem: The Banach contraction mapping theorem requires the map $T: X \to X$ to satisfy:

options.text: $\|Tx - Ty\| \le k\|x-y\|$ for some fixed $k < 1$ and all $x, y$.
options.explanation: The contraction condition with $k < 1$ ensures successive iterates converge geometrically fast to the unique fixed point.
The theorem applies to any contraction on a complete metric space, linear or not. The Picard iteration for ODEs uses a non-linear contraction.
Surjectivity is not required. The theorem only guarantees existence of a fixed point, not that $T$ maps onto all of $X$.
The theorem holds in any complete metric space, including infinite-dimensional Banach spaces. The infinite-dimensional case is where it is most useful.
